terms.comment: Vitruvius’s Latin adjective, made on Greek διαγώνιος. The diagonal itself is līnea diagōnālis; Vitruvius describes it as the line drawn ab angulō ad angulum, from corner to corner, which is also what to say to a child.

evidence: Vitr. 9 praef. 5: līnea ab angulō ad angulum diagōnios perdūcātur
terms.comment: The Greek adjective, declined in Greek, as Vitruvius uses it.

phrases.latin: Dūc līneam ab angulō ad angulum: duo triangula fīent.
phrases.english: Draw a line from corner to corner: you’ll get two triangles.

phrases.latin: in eō quadrātō, longō et lātō pedēs X quod fuerit, līnea ab angulō ad angulum diagōnios perdūcātur, utī dīvidantur duo trigōna aequā magnitūdine
phrases.english: in that square, which will be ten feet long and wide, let a diagonal line be drawn from corner to corner, so that two triangles of equal size are divided off

sources: Lewis & Short: diagonalis · Lewis & Short: diagonios
